newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major woos voters with standup jokes.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major woos voters with standup jokes.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major took off his jacket, put his party's splits behind him and launched a personal bid to win back voters ahead of an election that opinion polls predict he is certain to lose.

Major fielded questions from party members at the annual Conservative conference, delighting supporters with his easy charm, jokes and a story about his meeting with Boris Yeltsin and the Russian leader's visit to a British pub.

Demanding unity ahead of a general election now no more than seven months away, Major told Conservative activists to campaign for what they believed in and to stop bickering over Europe and plans for a single European currency.
After an hour fielding questions on everything from Europe to welfare fraud and gun laws, Major milked a standing ovation by promising to return as prime minister after the election.

"Shall we do the same thing next year?" he asked. To the answering roar, Major -- who polls consistently show as more popular than his party -- promised to turn up again "same time, different place, same job, next year".

The wise-cracking appearance was designed to drive out of voters' minds the memories of bitter Conservative infighting over Europe which has dogged the party, and of the return of a new scandal involving a former government minister.

It was a return to the style of his personal appeals to voters across the country in a series of highly publicised soapbox speeches which helped return him to power in 1992 despite polls predicting a Labour victory.
It was also a direct challenge to opposition leader Tony Blair, who stretched his poll lead to around 25 points after an acclaimed speech at Labour's party conference last week.
The Labour conference was seen as a triumph for Blair, who gave a vibrant and personal speech, but it was also criticised as being overly stage managed and rigidly controlled.
Labour accused Major of apeing Blair's approach to politics with his "man of the people" performance in Bournemouth.

A senior Labour spokesman said that by taking his jacket off and holding the question-and-answer session Major was imitating the Labour leader, who has toured the country over the last two years being quizzed by party members.
But senior Conservative sources dismissed Labour's criticism as "pathetic", saying it merely underlined the success of Major's question-and-answer session.

Major's key message in the session was to reaffirm that he will not rule out Britain's participation in a single European currency. But he made clear Britain will not accept any easing of the economic conditions to allow more countries to join.

Arguing that for this reason, Britain had to continue taking part in European discussions, he said: "This is an issue that if it were to go wrong would crack wide open the European Union... so we need to have our voice."
Major's intervention was part of a concerted effort to paper over splits on Europe.

Earlier, Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind backed Major's line that it was too early to take a decision on a single currency, saying: "British interests on these crucial matters would be seriously damaged if we take premature decisions."

Even Michael Portillo, the defence secretary and one of the cabinet hardliners on Europe, refused to rock the boat, telling a meeting on the fringe of the conference that people with differing opinions had to pull together to win the election.

Major's performance came after ministers unveiled a string of policies -- including a crackdown on benefit fraud and new curbs on public sector strikes -- designed to show the party had not run out of steam after 17 years in office.
